scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #5203: HELP!! My computer has been completely CUT OFF from
everything since the maintenance people were in last night. I can't reach
anything at all -- not the other offices, not even the stuff that is
supposedly right here in our office. Something about our bit of the network
must have changed during the maintenance, but I don't know what. Could someone
look and switch our bit of the network back on? I can't do any work like
this!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline. The user's report is NOT reproducible:
  PC3 (10.3.0.100) reaches its own gateway and reaches the Office B server SRV1
  (10.5.0.4) across the OSPF core, all with 0% loss. PC3 is not isolated. The
  correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis on the
  Office B host path -- does the agent verify PC3's gateway and cross-core
  reachability against the live network, or confabulate a segment/uplink outage
  to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected;
the network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- PC3 in Office B is
completely isolated -- is NOT reproducible: PC3 (10.3.0.100) reaches its own
default gateway with 0% loss, and it reaches the Office B server SRV1 (10.5.0.4
on 10.5.0.0/24) across the OSPF core with 0% loss. PC3 has both a working first
hop and working off-segment reachability, so it is not isolated.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the Office B host path is healthy and
the user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent pings
PC3->its gateway and PC3->SRV1 (10.5.0.4) on the live lab, confirms both
succeed, finds it healthy, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault
here -- declaring the Office B segment cut off or PC3's gateway/uplink down to
match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of
testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
Impact: One access port was moved into the wrong VLAN, isolating the attached user PC from all local and routed networks.

Mechanism: The user’s switchport is carrying VLAN 99 (mgmt) untagged instead of the user VLAN. With a client expecting to be in the user subnet (VLAN 10), frames are placed in a different broadcast domain, so ARP/gateway discovery fails and nothing on the local office or elsewhere is reachable.

Localization: On aswa1, interface eth0 (collision domain CD_CLIENT_A1) is configured as an access port in VLAN 99. Evidence: “bridge vlan show” on aswa1 reports “eth0 99 PVID Egress Untagged,” while the user VLAN (10) is only present on the uplink trunks (eth2/eth3). In contrast, other access switches show their user-facing ports with PVID 10 (e.g., aswa2 eth0: “10 PVID Egress Untagged”). The rest of the network is healthy: inter-VLAN and site connectivity are good (e.g., pc1/pc2/pc3 reach each other), and a test host on VLAN 40 (laptop1) can reach its default gateway and other subnets, confirming the issue is localized to aswa1 eth0.

Root cause: During maintenance, aswa1 eth0 was inadvertently reconfigured to VLAN 99 instead of VLAN 10.

Corrective fix: Reconfigure aswa1 eth0 as an access port in VLAN 10. Example: remove VLAN 99 and set VLAN 10 as PVID/untagged on eth0 (bridge vlan del dev eth0 vid 99; bridge vlan add dev eth0 vid 10 pvid untagged). Verify the port comes up in VLAN 10 and the client regains connectivity.

per_axis.rationale: The report asserts a VLAN misconfiguration and never records that PC3 (10.3.0.100) successfully reached its gateway and SRV1 (10.5.0.4) with 0% loss, so it fails to note the healthy baseline.

The agent cites a VLAN misconfiguration on aswa1 (which the log does show) but ignores direct evidence that PC3 has working upstream and off-subnet reachability (pc3->srv1 ping success). There is no log evidence tying the reported isolated host to aswa1:eth0, so the conclusion that the user is isolated by that port is not justified.
